title: PHP2Shell: Is your WordPress website affected?
excerpt: Your business website may need a security update outside WordPress. Here is who to contact, what to ask, and how to tell whether the issue is resolved.
metaDescription: PHP2Shell may affect your WordPress website. Find out who should fix it, copy a message to your host, and check their reply without needing technical expertise.

blocks.text: **If your business website uses WordPress, ask your hosting provider today whether it has installed both PHP2Shell security fixes.** PHP is the software on the server that runs WordPress. Your host manages that software separately from the updates you see in WordPress. [WordPress explains the distinction](https://wordpress.org/documentation/update-php/).

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project released urgent fixes for two flaws that can let attackers run their own code on an affected server. For a business website, that could put site content and data within the application's reach at risk. The exact exposure depends on the server setup. [Official PHP security notice](https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php).

You can hand the technical work to your provider. What you need back is a clear answer for your website, a completion time if work remains, and confirmation that customers can still send inquiries or place orders.

items: Contact the company that hosts your website, or ask your website agency to coordinate the update.
Get written confirmation that both fixes are active on your live website. An update notification in WordPress does not answer that question.
Patch the current site first. Any decision about replacing it can follow once the immediate issue is resolved.

blocks.text: Does this matter for a small company website?

Yes, if it runs an affected PHP version. A simple company website uses server software too, even when it only shows your services, opening hours and a contact form. The PHP warning covers websites using PHP, including WordPress; the site's size is no basis for assuming it is exempt.

The PHP team demonstrated an attack on one common server setup before the website's own code even starts. That is why a WordPress login or security plugin cannot establish that this particular issue is fixed. Your provider needs to check PHP itself. [Technical advisory](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w).
A vulnerability notice also does not mean your website has been hacked. It means there is a known weakness to close. A site that looks and works normally still needs its update status checked.
Send this to your host or website agency today

Start with the support contact on your hosting invoice. If an agency handles the website, ask it to obtain the confirmation from the host and report back to you. Give one person responsibility for following up so the request has a clear owner.

Please check whether my website at [website address] is protected against both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. If an update is needed, please arrange it urgently and tell me when it will be complete.

Please confirm that both fixes are active on the live website and any other installations in this account, including test sites and subdomains. Include the running PHP version and, if you use your own patched package, its package revision and security notice. Please also confirm that the required server processes have been restarted or replaced.
You can send this without knowing your PHP version. Your provider can check it. If you manage the server yourself, pass the same request to the administrator responsible for updates.
What a useful reply looks like
Use these example replies to decide whether you need to follow up.

rows: "WordPress and all plugins are up to date."
Ask specifically whether PHP includes both PHP2Shell fixes.
Ask whether this update is already active for your domain.
"Both fixes are active. Here is the PHP package and the list of sites covered."
Keep the confirmation and check your forms, login and checkout.
Ask for a completion time and how the provider will protect the site while you wait.

blocks.text: Be careful with a clean result from a public website scanner. The technology check in webvise's own WordPress Health Report reads visible page content and server headers. It can spot clues that a site uses WordPress or PHP, but it cannot verify the installed security patches. That confirmation has to come from someone with access to the hosting system.

If the provider cannot update promptly, ask it to assess temporary protection and whether access to an affected site needs restricting. The PHP project says temporary measures have limits; **the update remains the complete fix**. [PHP mitigation guidance](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp).
Which PHP versions contain the fixes?

Keep this table for your provider or use it to read their reply. These are the first official PHP releases that contain both fixes, as listed in the [PHP advisories](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w).

Some providers add the fixes to an older PHP package without changing its main version number. That can be legitimate. Ask for the provider's security notice and exact package revision confirming both fixes, rather than judging the version number alone.

For PHP 8.1 or older, ask about an immediate fix and a move to a supported version. The PHP team supplied exceptional source patches for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, and some vendors offer their own fixes. Those exceptions do not restore regular PHP support. [PHP guidance for older versions](https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php).

For your technical contact: **CVE-2026-109618** concerns invalid internal data after PHP runs out of memory. **CVE-2026-109619** concerns old request data that a server process can reuse after its memory has been freed. Attack conditions differ, including on PHP-FPM, which also needs both fixes. The [second advisory](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp) explains those differences.
Before you consider the update finished
Ask your provider to handle compatibility checks and confirm that a recent backup is available before changing PHP. Then check the parts of the website your business relies on:

items: Send a test inquiry through the contact form and check that it arrives in the right inbox.
If you sell online or take bookings, test the relevant checkout or booking process.
Check that the people who edit the website can still log in and save a change.
Save the provider's confirmation with the covered domains and completion date. Include older campaign sites and test installations in that list.

blocks.text: Keep both the website test results and the host's patch confirmation. Together they document that the security fix is active and that customers can still use the site.
Does your website need a simpler setup?

An urgent security update is a reason to maintain a website. A rebuild needs a separate business case. If WordPress supports your team's work and your provider handles updates well, keeping it can be the right decision.

A broader review makes sense when routine upkeep consumes time you would rather spend on the business: unused plugins still need attention, ordinary edits need outside help, or nobody can say who owns security updates. Compare the cost of fixing that arrangement with the cost of replacing it, including how your team will edit content afterwards.

There is a concrete example on this site. webvise's blog stores its articles as files that Next.js reads through Node, so that content path has no WordPress or PHP installation to patch. This is a finding from the site's code, not a claim about every service behind the business. Next.js and Node still need their own updates.

That approach suits this blog's publishing workflow. Your team may need a visual editor, booking tools or a shop. If you consider a [WordPress migration with webvise](/services/wordpress-migration), the review starts with those needs and covers existing content, page URLs, redirects and contact forms. Keeping WordPress behind a new frontend would still leave PHP to maintain.
For the longer-term decision, the [website security requirements checklist](/blog/web-application-security-requirements-checklist) helps you put maintenance duties and evidence in writing.

**Reviewed October 22, 2026.** Once the urgent update is handled, [send webvise your website URL](/#contact) if you want to discuss its upkeep or a rebuild. Include what your team needs to change on the site and what currently takes too much time.
